answer.evidence: The width profile runs 8, 12, then 14 for rows 2-7, and then drops straight to 10 at row 8. The cap is rounded only at its upper corners and ends flat on the shaft, so it is a hat rather than an ellipse plate, which would narrow again below its widest rows. The white face carries a face-on ring symbol, and rows 6-7 are a teal underside, so the cap reads as a front-facing sign box. It has no front-edge line and no back-to-front ellipse profile. The shaft (rows 8-27) and the base (rows 26-29, width 14) are drawn only as vertical faces, with no horizontal top surface visible. The whole object reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small pole-like sign prop: a pale cap, a dark sign face with a yellow number mark, and a slim grey-blue post. It has 12 visible tones per full tile, equal to kiosk-a (12), above bus-shelter-a (6), and below vending-a (20). Near-flat coverage is 15%, higher than all references (0-9%) but small for a thin prop. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted, a dark blue-grey that follows the material, not black. Shading is about 4 steps on the post and cap against about 5 on the references. The post and lower body are fairly plain, with little grain or per-part highlighting. The 12 tones sit in the same range as the shipped references. By eye, though, it looks a little thinner and flatter than kiosk-a and vending-a, which carry more panel detail and highlights, so density is slightly lower. It would not be unacceptable beside bus-shelter-a, but with doubts it is borderline, and when in doubt it fails.
